lessonActivities.title: Gerund vs Infinitive: Basics and Key Difference
lessonActivities.content:
In English, some verbs are followed by a gerund (verb + -ing), and others by an infinitive (to + verb). Some verbs can take both with meaning change.

Gerund: enjoy doing, avoid doing, imagine doing.

Infinitive: want to do, plan to do, need to do.
examples: He wants to read the book. (infinitive)
lessonActivities.tips: Gerund often follows verbs of likes/dislikes. Infinitive often follows verbs of intentions or plans.

lessonActivities.title: After Certain Verbs: Gerund or Infinitive
lessonActivities.content:
Verbs like enjoy, avoid, mind are followed by gerunds. Verbs like want, hope, decide are followed by infinitives.

Some verbs can use both, e.g. like, love, start, with small nuance.
lessonActivities.tips: When your sentence is about preference or emotion, usually choose gerund. When it’s about plan or future action, choose infinitive.

lessonActivities.title: Bare Infinitive & Special Structures
lessonActivities.content:
Certain verbs like make, let, help, see, hear use a bare infinitive (without 'to').

Example: She made him study. I saw her leave. (not 'to leave')
lessonActivities.tips: Look for verbs of perception or permission to choose bare infinitive.

lessonActivities.title: Gerund vs Infinitive Meaning Change
lessonActivities.content:
Some verbs can have both forms but the meaning shifts. Example:

  • "remember to call" (don't forget future action)
  • "remember calling" (recollect past action)

Other pairs: stop, try, start, continue.
examples: I stopped smoking. (got rid of habit)
I stopped to smoke. (paused to have a cigarette)
lessonActivities.tips: When in doubt, compare with whether action is ongoing (gerund) or a specific future action (infinitive).

lessonActivities.title: Expressions and Prepositions with Gerund
lessonActivities.content: Some expressions are followed by gerund: 'no use', 'no point in', 'it's worth', 'can't help'. Prepositions always take gerund: 'after', 'before', 'instead of', 'good at'.
examples: She is interested in learning Spanish.
lessonActivities.tips: Rules of thumb: expressions + gerund; after preposition + gerund.

writingActivities.question: Write 5 sentences describing your favorite hobbies using gerunds.
writingActivities.hint: Use verbs like enjoy, love, like, dislike, avoid with '-ing'.

writingActivities.question: Write 5 sentences about future plans using infinitive (to + base verb).
writingActivities.hint: Use verbs like want, plan, hope, decide, intend.

writingActivities.question: Write 4 sentences that show the difference between gerund and infinitive for the same verb (start, continue, remember).
writingActivities.hint: Example: I remember meeting him vs I remembered to call.

writingActivities.question: Write 4 sentences using a bare infinitive with verbs like let/make/help/see/hear.
writingActivities.hint: Example: She made me clean my room. (not 'to clean')

writingActivities.question: Write 4 sentences using prepositions + gerund (after, before, instead of, good at, interested in).
writingActivities.hint: Example: Before leaving, I turn off the lights.

quizActivities.question: Gerund or infinitive?
quizActivities.sentence: I hope ___ a promotion next year.

quizActivities.question: Meaning difference: gerund vs infinitive
quizActivities.sentence: I forgot ___ the door when I left.
quizActivities.explanation: Forgot to lock = failed to do something.

quizActivities.question: Expression with gerund
quizActivities.sentence: It’s no point in ___ more coffee.
quizActivities.explanation: After no point in, use gerund (drinking).

spellingActivities.clue: I remember ___ my father at home.
